title: Asking AI About Health
hook: AI beats frantic late-night symptom-googling for calm, readable explanations — and makes a great prep tool for a doctor's visit. What it can't do is examine you or diagnose you.
key_points: Good for understanding conditions, decoding medical jargon, and prepping questions.
It can't examine you, doesn't know your history, and can be confidently wrong.
Don't use it to self-diagnose or to decide on medications or treatments.
In an emergency, call emergency services — not a chatbot.
content_html: Almost everyone has fallen down a late-night symptom-search rabbit hole and emerged convinced of the worst. A chatbot can actually be an improvement on that experience — not because it's more authoritative, but because it's calmer and clearer. Ask it to explain a diagnosis your doctor mentioned, translate the jargon on a lab report, describe what a procedure involves, or lay out general lifestyle factors for a condition, and you'll usually get a readable, balanced overview that helps you feel less lost. It's especially valuable as a preparation tool: have it help you write down the right questions to ask at an appointment, so your limited time with a clinician is well spent.
extra_html: But the boundary here is a matter of safety, not etiquette. A general chatbot is not a doctor. It cannot examine you, run tests, or see the dozens of subtle cues a clinician uses; it doesn't know your medical history; and it can produce a confident, plausible answer that's flat wrong — including inventing conditions, dosages, or interactions. So use it to understand and prepare, never to diagnose or treat. Don't let it talk you into or out of seeing a professional, and never act on its advice about medications, doses, or whether a symptom is serious. Above all, it has no place in an emergency: chest pain, difficulty breathing, signs of a stroke, thoughts of self-harm, or any urgent situation mean you call emergency services or get to care right away. Think of AI as a knowledgeable friend who's read a lot — helpful for getting oriented, but no substitute for the doctor who can actually look at you.

related.title: AI in Healthcare
related.hook: AI can spot a tumor on a scan faster than a tired radiologist and flag patterns no one would catch by eye. It's a powerful assistant to doctors — not a replacement for one.

related.title: When AI Makes Things Up
related.hook: AI 'hallucinations' aren't glitches — they're the technology working as designed. A model that always predicts a plausible next word will sometimes produce a plausible falsehood.

related.title: What AI Can't Do
related.hook: Today's AI can write a sonnet and flunk a question a child gets right. Knowing its hard edges — no real understanding, no live truth, no common sense — is what makes you good at using it.

flashcards.prompt: What's an appropriate way to use AI for health?

choices.text: Understanding a condition and preparing questions for your doctor
Getting a firm diagnosis instead of seeing a doctor
Deciding which prescription medication to take

flashcards.explanation_html: AI is a good explainer and prep tool. It can't examine you, lacks your history, and may be wrong — so diagnosis and treatment belong to a clinician.

flashcards.prompt: What should you do in a medical emergency?
flashcards.back_html: Call emergency services or get to care immediately — never rely on a chatbot to assess an urgent or life-threatening situation.
